hints: Copying a struct copies its data; copying a class variable copies a reference.
exercises.solution: `Move` receives a copy of the struct and changes the copy, so `a.Value` stays 1. `Shift` receives a copy of the reference to the one `Box` object and changes that object, so `b.Value` becomes 11. Output: `1 11`.

feedback.message: Not yet — record equality compares each property with its own `Equals`. How do two different arrays compare?
Not yet — `with { }` makes a shallow copy. Which array does `z.Players` refer to?

hints: Arrays compare by reference, and `with` copies references, not the arrays they point to.
exercises.solution: `x` and `y` have equal names but two *different* arrays, and arrays compare by reference, so `x == y` is `False`. `x with { }` is a shallow copy: `z.Players` is the very same array as `x.Players`, so every property compares equal and `x == z` is `True`. Output: `False True`. Moral: keep collections out of records, or use immutable collections with value equality.

Field and property initialisers run before the constructor body.

`q` is a copy of `p` with `Age` set to 31. A record's generated `ToString` prints the type name and its public properties in braces:

exercises.prompt: You need a type for a geographic coordinate: a latitude and a longitude, both `double`, never changed after creation, created millions of times in a mapping engine, and compared by value. What is the best declaration?

options.label: `readonly record struct Coordinate(double Latitude, double Longitude);`
options.feedback: Yes. It is small (16 bytes), immutable and a single conceptual value, so a value type avoids millions of heap allocations, and `record` gives value equality and a readable `ToString` for free.

options.label: `class Coordinate { public double Latitude; public double Longitude; }`
options.feedback: Not yet — this is mutable, uses public fields, compares by reference, and allocates every coordinate on the heap.

options.label: `struct Coordinate { public double Latitude { get; set; } public double Longitude { get; set; } }`
options.feedback: Not yet — a value type is right, but this one is mutable, which invites the classic bug of changing a copy.

options.label: `abstract class Coordinate` with `Latitude` and `Longitude` in derived classes
options.feedback: Not yet — there is no family of kinds of coordinate here, so inheritance adds complexity with no benefit.

hints: Check the .NET guidance: small, immutable, single value, created in large numbers.
Which option is both a value type and immutable?
exercises.solution: A `readonly record struct` fits every requirement: it is a value type (no heap allocation per coordinate), `readonly` makes it immutable, and `record` generates value equality, `GetHashCode`, `ToString` and deconstruction.

exercises.prompt: Given `record Booking { public required string Guest { get; init; } }`, which lines compile? (Choose all that apply.)

options.label: `var b = new Booking { Guest = "Ana" };`
options.feedback: Yes. An object initializer may set an `init` property, and it satisfies `required`.

options.label: `var b = new Booking();`
options.feedback: Not yet — `Guest` is `required`, so the compiler insists that the initializer sets it.

options.label: `b.Guest = "Bea";` on an existing booking `b`
options.feedback: Not yet — `init` properties can be set only during construction (constructor or initializer), never afterwards.

options.label: `var c = b with { Guest = "Bea" };` on an existing booking `b`
options.feedback: Yes. A `with` expression creates a new record and may set its `init` properties, leaving `b` unchanged.

hints: `init` means "settable while the object is being created".
exercises.solution: (a) and (d) compile. (a) sets the required property in an initializer. (d) creates a new record via `with`, which counts as initialisation. (b) fails because `Guest` is required, and (c) fails because `init` properties cannot be assigned after construction.
